strengths: Addresses an important open problem: Best-of-Both-Worlds (BoBW) guarantees for episodic MDPs with heavy-tailed losses, for both known and unknown transitions.

Proposes novel algorithms HT-FTRL-OM and HT-FTRL-UOB that integrate FTRL over occupancy measures, 1/α-Tsallis entropy regularization, skipping loss estimators, and a pessimistic estimator with upper occupancy bounds.

Achieves strong theoretical guarantees: adversarial regret O(T^{1/α}) for known transitions and O(T^{1/α}+√T) for unknown transitions, while obtaining logarithmic (or polylogarithmic) instance-dependent regret in self-bounding/stochastic regimes.

Introduces several nontrivial technical innovations, including local control of shifted losses under heavy tails, a suboptimal mass propagation principle, and a regret decomposition that isolates transition uncertainty from heavy-tailed estimation and skipping bias.
Provides detailed proofs in the appendix, carefully handling negative heavy-tailed losses and the coupling introduced by state transitions.
The results recover known BoBW bounds for bounded losses when α=2 and match known adversarial lower bounds up to logarithmic factors.
weaknesses: Some technical inconsistencies and typos appear in the appendix. For example, Lemma B.10 uses a factor H^α S^{1-α} whereas the derivation in Lemma B.9 suggests H^{1/α} S^{1-1/α}; the constant factor in Eq. (43) seems off; and the learning rate definition in Algorithm 1 vs. Lemma B.9 appears to have a missing β factor. These affect explicit polynomial constants but not the main T-dependence.
The algorithms require prior knowledge of the tail parameters α and σ, which limits practical applicability. A parameter-free extension is not provided.
No lower bounds are established for the self-bounding regime, so the optimality of the logarithmic instance-dependent rates is not fully justified.
The polynomial dependence on H, S, and A is quite large (e.g., H^{α+1} factors), which may limit practical relevance, although the paper focuses on T-dependence.
The paper lacks empirical validation, which is acceptable for a theory paper but could have helped illustrate the algorithms' behavior.

Some claims of being the 'first' could be more carefully qualified in light of prior instance-dependent heavy-tailed RL work, though the paper argues that existing instance-dependent guarantees are polynomial in T rather than logarithmic.

strengths: Addresses a legitimate and well-motivated open problem: achieving Best-of-Both-Worlds (BoBW) guarantees for episodic MDPs with heavy-tailed (α-moment bounded) losses, a regime that prior HTMDP work has not handled adaptively.

Provides the first BoBW algorithms for HTMDPs in both the known-transition (HT-FTRL-OM) and unknown-transition (HT-FTRL-UOB) settings, with plausible rate trade-offs: Õ(T^{1/α}) adversarial / O(log T) self-bounding for known transitions, and Õ(T^{1/α}+√T) adversarial / O(log² T) self-bounding for unknown transitions. These reduce correctly to the bounded-loss BoBW results of Jin & Luo (2020) / Jin et al. (2021) at α=2.

Contains genuinely novel technical components, in particular the local (pointwise and second-moment) control of the heavy-tailed shifted/skipped loss (Lemma 4.2, Lemma 4.3), which is what makes the skipping estimator compatible with the loss-shifting argument over occupancy measures.

The paper is clearly written and well structured, with the regret decomposition (stability / penalty / skipping error, and TransErr / EstReg / SkipErr / PessErr) laid out explicitly, and it honestly flags that the poly(H,S,A) dependence is loose.

The self-bounding bound recovers the gap-dependence structure of the heavy-tailed bandit lower bounds (ω_Δ(α)=Σ Δ^{-1/(α-1)}, σ^{α/(α-1)}), suggesting the instance-dependent rates are of the right form.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely incremental. The algorithmic backbone is directly inherited: FTRL over occupancy measures with Tsallis entropy (Jin & Luo 2020; Jin et al. 2021), the skipping estimator (Huang et al. 2022), doubling-epoch estimation and Bernstein confidence sets (Jin et al. 2020), and the self-bounding machinery (Jin et al. 2021). The main new ingredient is layering a skipping estimator onto this framework. The claimed "new suboptimal-mass propagation principle" is in fact explicitly adapted from Jin et al. (2021, Lemma 20) ("Following Lemma 20 in Jin et al. (2021), we derive the following lemma"), so presenting it as a novel principle overstates the contribution.

The harder (unknown-transition) case is proved by repeatedly deferring to prior work: e.g., "By the analysis in Jin et al. (2021, Eqs. (36-38))", "By similar argument in Lemma B.6", "By the same process in Appendix B.3 in Jin et al. (2021)". Because the heavy-tailed skipping error is precisely where the new difficulty lies, this makes it hard to verify that the extension is actually correct and limits reproducibility of the central claim.

There are apparent errors/inconsistencies that undermine confidence. In Lemma B.10 the bound Σ_s (x_t(s)-ρ(s))_+^{1/α} ≤ H^α S^{1-α} Σ_sub x_t^{1/α} contradicts the (correct) H^{1/α} S^{1-1/α} factor derived by the identical argument in Lemma B.9; yet the erroneous H^α S^{1-α} factor is carried into M in Theorem B.1. Also, Algorithm 2's learning rate η_t = (σ(t-t_i+1)^{1/α})^{-1} omits the β constant that Theorem C.1 and Lemma C.8 explicitly rely on for the local-stability condition.

The adversarial bound in Theorem 5.1 is written as Õ(T^{1/α}+√T), but for α∈(1,2] one always has T^{1/α} ≥ √T, so the √T term is redundant; this suggests the authors have not fully pinned down the true rate structure. Similarly, the "matching" of the bandit lower bound is asserted rather than derived for the MDP case.

The polynomial factors are extremely loose (e.g., A^{5-4/α}, S^{2-1/α}, H^{α+1}, and H^{α²/(α-1)+1} in the self-bounding unknown-transition bound). While the BoBW-MDP literature does hide such factors, the exponents here are large and unoptimized, reducing the practical meaning of the rates and making it hard to compare against competitors.

No empirical validation is provided (understandable for a theory paper), and the algorithms assume knowledge of the tail parameters (α, σ) and require solving a convex FTRL problem over the occupancy polytope (plus Comp-UOB) per episode, which is only loosely addressed.

strengths: Addresses a natural and well-motivated open problem—Best-of-Both-Worlds guarantees for episodic MDPs with heavy-tailed (bounded α-moment) losses—and provides the first such results for both known and unknown transitions. This is a meaningful extension of BoBW theory beyond the bounded/sub-Gaussian regime.

The technical toolkit is genuinely novel and non-trivial: (i) an occupancy-based skipping loss estimator with occupancy-dependent thresholds τ_t(s,a)=Cσt^{1/α}x_t(s,a)^{1/α} and matching skipping bonus b_t^{skip}, whose bias-compensation is correctly calibrated (E[|ℓ|1[|ℓ|>τ]] ≤ σ^α τ^{1-α} = b_t^{skip}); (ii) a local pointwise control of the shifted heavy-tailed loss (Lemma 4.2) via decomposition into a centered term and a differential value function term, plus the corresponding second-moment bound (Lemma 4.3); and (iii) the suboptimal-mass propagation principle (Lemma 4.4) that lets the penalty and skipping terms be restricted to suboptimal actions, enabling O(log T) self-bounding regret.

The algorithm/analysis correctly handles negative losses with no non-negativity assumption (unlike some prior heavy-tailed BoBW bandit work), and the derived bounds reduce to the standard bounded-loss BoBW rates when α=2, and to Bubeck et al.'s heavy-tailed bandit lower bounds in the single-state reduction—good sanity checks on the exponents.

The regret decompositions are well-structured. The known-transition decomposition (Stability/Penalty/Skipping) and the unknown-transition four-way split (TransErr/EstReg/SkipErr/PessErr) are sensibly organized so that each piece is controlled by an appropriate tool (FTRL stability, self-bounding terms, Bernstein confidence widths, UOB residual argument). The main results are internally consistent between the main text (Theorems 4.1, 5.1) and the appendix (Theorems B.1, C.1) with respect to the T-dependence.
The paper is generally well organized and the challenge/insight roadmap in Section 4.2 and 5.2 helps the reader follow a technically dense argument.
weaknesses: The polynomial factors in H,S,A are extremely loose, and some explicit order computations appear inconsistent. In particular, Eq. (14) states the second self-bounding term as M^{α/(1-α)}σ^{α/(1-α)}ω_Δ(α)log T, whereas the derivation of Eq. (42) gives M^{α/(α-1)}σ^{α/(α-1)}ω_Δ(α)log T; Eq. (15)'s claimed order H^{(2α²-α)/(α-1)}S^αA^{2α-1} does not match the order implied by M=O(H^{α+1-1/α}S^{1-1/α}A^{3-3/α}) either. These do not affect the T-dependence that carries the main claim, but they signal that the explicit bookkeeping was not carefully verified.

The pessimism argument (Lemma C.4) appears to be off by a constant: with B_i(s,a)=min{1,Σ_{s'}B_i(s,a,s')} and D=Hσ, the bound Σ_{s'}(P̂-P)[s'|s,a]·E[V^P] ≤ D·B_i(s,a) can fail when the confidence widths are large (e.g., unvisited (s,a) with Σ_{s'}B_i(s,a,s')≥1 and Σ_{s'}|P̂-P| up to 2), suggesting D should be ≥2Hσ. This is a constant-factor issue rather than an asymptotic one, but it needs to be corrected/justified.

Large parts of the unknown-transition analysis are delegated to 'similar to Jin et al. (2021)' (TransErr, the G_1/G_2/G_3 self-bounding terms, the UOB residual argument, Lemma C.8's EstReg). Because the estimator here uses UOB importance weights 1/u_t, skipping, and an extra -D·B_i penalty, the transfer is not automatic, and the manuscript does not verify that the prior-work lemmas remain valid under heavy-tailed, unbounded losses. This makes the central proof difficult to check and leaves a real verification burden unaddressed.

The text overstates the stochastic-regime conclusion for the unknown-transition case: it claims the instance-dependent bound is 'exactly' O(poly(H,S,A)σ^{α/(α-1)}ω_Δ(α)log²T), but Theorem 5.1/C.1 also contains σ²ω_Δ(2)log T and σ²Δ_min^{-1}log T terms that do not vanish in the stochastic regime; the claim should be qualified.

The algorithms require prior knowledge of the tail parameters (α, σ) and specific tuning constants (C, β, D), with no parameter-free/adaptive variant, which limits the practical reach relative to recent parameter-free heavy-tailed BoBW bandit work.

Minor typographical/carelessness issues (e.g., 'C_ab' for C_sb in Section 4.1, 't_t^{skip}' for ℓ_t^{skip} in Appendix B.3, P̂/F notation inconsistencies in Appendix C.3) that add friction to verification.
